# RG03 `deployer-is-attacker`: The exploit runs as the contract that deployed the protocol

<!-- Generated by `realism-gate explain --markdown`. Do not edit by hand. -->

**Severity:** warn (warn)

The test contract deploys the code under review in setUp() and then calls it without changing sender, so every call runs as the deployer.

## Why it matters

Constructors commonly give the deployer ownership or every role. A test that deploys with `new Vault()` and then calls `vault.sweep()` from the test contract has proved that the deployer can sweep. Whether an outsider can is untested. This is the single most common way an honest PoC accidentally proves a privileged action.

## How to fix it

Deploy and configure as one address, attack as another: `vm.startPrank(attacker)` before the exploit steps, or transfer ownership to a dedicated owner in `setUp()`.

## Fires on

```solidity
function setUp() public { vault = new Vault(); }
function test_sweep() public {
    vault.sweep(address(token)); // runs as the deployer
}
```

## Does not fire on

```solidity
function setUp() public { vault = new Vault(); }
function test_sweep() public {
    vm.prank(attacker);
    vault.sweep(address(token));
}
```

## Known false-positive modes

- A contract with no access control at all, where the deployer has no extra power. The finding is still worth an `allow` comment saying so, because the triager will ask.
- A constructor that hands ownership to an argument that the tool does not read as privileged. Pass a variable named for the role (`owner`, `admin`) or label it.

## Silencing it

Add a comment on the line, or the line above, with a reason:

```solidity
// realism-gate: allow(RG03) <why this is not a defect here>
```

A comment without a reason is ignored, and the output says so.
